text:
Alice Chen: Quick design q — for Redwood Private envelope encryption, what's our plan for KMS call frequency? Should we unwrap DEKs on every request, cache them per-process, or keep long-lived DEKs encrypted and only call KMS on rotate?
Raj Patel: Strong +1 for KEK/DEK separation. KEK stays in KMS, DEK used for actual data. We should avoid hitting KMS on every request. Cache DEKs in memory with a short TTL and strict ACLs.
Miguel Alvarez: Curious about threat model — if process memory is compromised, cached DEKs leak. Are we comfortable with that risk for Dedicated pods? Maybe use mlock + in-process hardware-backed keystore where available.
Lisa Wong: For Private (on-prem) customers we can't assume HSM. Proposal: default cache TTL = 5m, configurable per-tenant, with option for no-cache for high-security tenants. Also keep LRU cache size limit and zero memory on eviction.
Alice Chen: That matches what I was thinking. Also need to handle rotation: when KEK rotates, we must rewrap active DEKs or mark them stale. How aggressive should rewrap be?
Raj Patel: Rewrap lazily: keep DEKs wrapped with previous KEK until next unwrap, then rewrap with new KEK. Immediate bulk rewrap is costly and hits KMS. But record rewrap-required flag in metadata so we can audit and schedule background rewrap.
Miguel Alvarez: Note: lazy rewrap means if KEK is compromised and rotated, DEKs still encrypted under old KEK until next use. Acceptable only if rotation is a precaution, not a response to confirmed compromise. For confirmed compromise, we need emergency bulk rewrap or re-encryption flow.
Lisa Wong: Agree. So two modes: graceful rotation (lazy rewrap) and emergency rotation (force rewrap). Emergency should trigger a job that unwraps & rewraps, with rate-limited KMS calls and monitoring.
security-bot: FYI — internal runbook link: https://redwood.internal/runbooks/kms-rotation (permissions required).
Raj Patel: KMS call frequency concerns: for read-heavy workloads batching doesn't help because unwrap is per-DEK. But we can cache DEKs per-process and share across threads. For cross-process sharing, use encrypted DEK store in redis? That still requires KMS to create/unwrap initial DEK. Cache validity must be tied to tenant policy.
Miguel Alvarez: If we store wrapped DEKs in Redis, ensure Redis encryption at rest + ACLs. Also set short TTLs for wrapped DEK cache to limit blast radius. Consider using envelope with AEAD (AES-GCM) for DEK usage to detect tampering.
Alice Chen: What about KMS cost & rate limits (AWS KMS has API limits)? We need bulk rewrap backoff strategy.
Raj Patel: Use exponential backoff + jitter for KMS calls. For scheduled rewrap jobs, distribute across time windows and use concurrency control per-KMS key. Also instrument per-key call counters and alert if near quota.
Lisa Wong: Multi-cloud: AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault all have slightly different semantics. For example, GCP supports asymmetric keys better? Need an adapter layer that normalizes wrap/unwrap and error codes.
Miguel Alvarez: Also consider using local key-cache with a proof-of-possession TTL: DEK encrypted with KEK, but processes store HMAC of DEK and verify before use. That helps detect unauthorized tampering when a wrapped DEK is restored from persistent cache.
Alice Chen: Audit logging: every wrap/unwrap must be logged with key id, tenant id, caller principal, and purpose. For Private, logs may be pushed to customer SIEM. Make sure we never log plaintext DEKs.
security-bot: Reminder — KMS access must be via short-lived IAM creds. See iam-policy doc: https://redwood.internal/policies/kms-iam
ops-oncall: One operational note: during bulk rewrap jobs we might spike KMS latency; add circuit-breaker to fallback to read-only mode (serve cached tokens) or degrade gracefully.
Raj Patel: Final sketch of defaults: cache_dek = true, cache_ttl = 300s, max_deks_per_process = 1000, rewrap_mode = "lazy", emergency_rewrap = manual with job, kms_backoff = exponential, audit = enabled. Configs per-tenant + env override.
Lisa Wong: I'll draft a short RFC with config knobs, threat model, and emergency runbook. Want to include code sample for cache config.
Alice Chen: Great — include migration plan for customers currently using always-unwrapped model. Also enumerate metrics: kms_calls/sec, cache_miss_rate, rewrap_jobs_pending, last_rewrap_time.
Miguel Alvarez: +1. Also test harness to simulate KEK rotation and compromised DEK scenarios.
Alice Chen: Thanks all — assign RFC to @Lisa and ops runbook to @Miguel. :thumbsup:
